newsitem.title: USA: MCI sees 1997, '98 earnings below hopes.
newsitem.headline: MCI sees 1997, '98 earnings below hopes.

text.p: MCI Communications Corp. said Thursday it expected earnings for the second half of 1997 and into 1998 to be below current Wall Street expectations due to delays in gaining entry into U.S. local phone service markets.
In a statement released after the market close Thursday, MCI said it expected earnings for the second quarter of 1997 to be in line with analyst expectations.
The First Call consensus estimate for the second quarter was 40 cents per share before the warning. The consensus estimates for 1997 as a whole stood at $1.66 per share and $1.89 for 1998.

The second largest U.S. long-distance company blamed the higher-than-expected losses on foot-dragging by regional Bell companies that dominate local service markets. MCI said the losses resulted from heavy investments it is making to extend its reach into this business.

Washington-based MCI said local market losses for the year could reach $800 million, more than twice what it had originally planned, and that the bulk of the losses will occur in the second half of the year due to the underutilization of investments MCI has made in local phone operations. It said 1998 losses in its local business could exceed the levels incurred in 1997.
MCI said it is experiencing ongoing competition in its core long-distance business and that pricing trends continued to decline.
In addition, MCI said its results are being hurt by redeployment of marketing, operations, and product development resources from its long-distance business to local phone operations.
Earlier, MCI stock fell 19 cents to $42.375 on Nasdaq.

MCI said it is also exploring a series of unspecified steps to improve its financial performance. It said no decisions have been finalised, but that they could result in material charges to MCI's 1997 results of operations.

"Regulators must move swiftly to remove the anti-competitive obstacles that are preventing local phone customers from enjoying lower prices, innovative products and better customer service," MCI President Timothy Price said.

In particular, MCI said its core revenue growth will suffer and profits decline in 1998 unless federal and state regulators take action to further open U.S. local phone markets to competition by new entrants such as MCI.
"In their efforts to delay local competition, the (Baby Bells) are obstructing the Telecom Act, sabotaging the FCC's objectives and undermining the power of Congress," he said.
MCI's determination to become a major player in local phone markets despite deep financial sacrifices is disappointing but hardly surprising, analysts said.
"They are making a strategic move," industry analyst Jeffrey Kagan said. "They are willing to bite the bullet for a little while."
